summary: KERNEL CONTEST: The Second Amendment text ('A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.') serves as the fixed substrate. Reading A (collective rights interpretation) views this as ensuring state militia capacity, with constraints focused on military-grade weapons and benefiting community safety through regulation. Reading B (individual rights interpretation) sees this as guaranteeing personal firearm ownership, creating constraints on government regulation and benefiting individual self-defense advocates while potentially increasing gun violence victims.

KERNEL CONTEST: The biblical covenant between God and Abraham in Genesis serves as the fixed substrate. Reading A (Jewish interpretation) sees this as establishing an exclusive covenant through Isaac, creating constraints on religious identity that benefit Jewish continuity while potentially excluding other claimants. Reading B (Islamic interpretation) views this as continuing through Ishmael, establishing constraints that validate Islamic prophetic lineage while challenging Jewish exclusivity claims. Each reading creates structurally different religious authority systems and beneficiary structures.

KERNEL CONTEST: The 1648 Peace of Westphalia establishing state sovereignty serves as the fixed substrate. Reading A (absolute sovereignty interpretation) views this as creating constraints against external interference in domestic affairs, benefiting state autonomy while potentially enabling human rights violations within borders. Reading B (responsibility to protect interpretation) sees sovereignty as conditional, creating constraints on state actions when human rights are threatened, benefiting international intervention advocates while potentially undermining state autonomy.

KERNEL CONTEST: The Geneva Conventions on wartime conduct serve as the fixed substrate. Reading A (state-centric interpretation) applies these constraints only to uniformed military forces, benefiting state actors while limiting protections for non-traditional combatants. Reading B (universal human rights interpretation) extends protections to all combatants, creating constraints on state military actions that benefit non-state actors while potentially reducing state military effectiveness.

KERNEL CONTEST: The Takings Clause ('nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation') serves as the fixed substrate. Reading A (narrow interpretation) constrains only direct physical appropriations, benefiting property owners with limited protections while enabling regulatory takings without compensation. Reading B (broad interpretation) constrains regulations that substantially diminish property value, benefiting property owners with expanded protections while potentially limiting government regulatory power for public welfare.

KERNEL CONTEST: The 1944 Bretton Woods agreement establishing the dollar-gold standard serves as the fixed substrate. Reading A (Keynesian interpretation) saw this as creating constraints on capital flows to protect domestic policy autonomy, benefiting national economic stability while limiting international finance. Reading B (neoliberal interpretation) emphasized convertibility and free markets, creating constraints on government intervention that benefited international capital mobility while potentially undermining domestic economic stability.

KERNEL CONTEST: The biblical texts regarding God's nature serve as the fixed substrate. Reading A (Trinitarian interpretation) sees God as three persons in one being, creating constraints on Christian orthodoxy that benefit institutional churches while excluding non-Trinitarian Christians. Reading B (Unitarian interpretation) views God as singular, creating constraints that reject Trinitarian hierarchy while benefiting biblical literalists and challenging institutional authority structures.

KERNEL CONTEST: The NPT text serves as the fixed substrate. Reading A (nuclear weapons states' interpretation) emphasizes non-proliferation constraints on non-nuclear states while maintaining disarmament as a distant goal, benefiting existing nuclear powers while constraining others. Reading B (non-nuclear states' interpretation) emphasizes Article VI disarmament obligations, creating constraints on nuclear weapons states while benefiting global security advocates and challenging nuclear hierarchies.

KERNEL CONTEST: The fair use provisions in copyright law serve as the fixed substrate. Reading A (creator-centric interpretation) creates narrow constraints on unauthorized use, benefiting rights holders and content industries while limiting transformative works. Reading B (user-centric interpretation) creates broader constraints on copyright enforcement, benefiting public domain advocates, remix culture, and educational use while potentially reducing creator compensation.

KERNEL CONTEST: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change text serves as the fixed substrate. Reading A (developed nations' interpretation) emphasizes voluntary commitments and technology transfer, creating constraints on binding emissions reductions that benefit industrialized economies while disproportionately impacting vulnerable nations. Reading B (developing nations' interpretation) emphasizes common but differentiated responsibilities, creating constraints on historical emissions that benefit climate justice while requiring greater sacrifices from developed economies.
